title: Omniscience — and the invitation of the gods, refused (3.49–3.51)
hook: discernment brings knowing everything, and the next step is letting even that go; then the gods arrive with an invitation, and the yogi says no

segments.voice: Yesterday: indriya-jaya, and your line, the senses. From the known to the knowing. Did you notice the tasting more than the taste? Today, the knower. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

The classical commentary tells it as a scene. A yogi sits in practice, far along now, close to the end. And the gods arrive. Not demons, not tempters in disguise. Gods, the beings of the high places, warm and respectful. Sir, sit here. Enjoy yourself here. This pleasure is lovely. This elixir holds back age and death. Here's a chariot that flies. Here are trees that grant every wish. Come and stay. Generous, polite, and sincere. Today's sutras say what the yogi does next.
screen: `THE GODS ARRIVE.` → `SIT HERE. ENJOY HERE.` → `COME AND STAY.`

segments.voice: First the summit. Sutra 3.49: for the one who sees only the difference between the mind's clearest part and the seer, mastery over all states of being, and knowing everything. Omniscience. Sarva-jnatritva. This is discernment, which we met three weeks ago, carried all the way. Then sutra 3.50, a bold line. By dispassion even toward that, the seeds of every fault are destroyed, and freedom comes. Kaivalya. Even toward that. Even omniscience gets set down. Then 3.51. When invited by those in the high places, don't be attached, and don't be proud, because unwanted things could return. Two dangers, not one. Attachment: you might say yes. And pride: you might say no, and then think, the gods themselves came to invite me. The commentary gives the yogi's answer as a reflection. I've been roasted on the coals of rebirth, tossed in the dark, and now I've found the lamp of yoga. Why would I let these sweet things be the wind that blows it out? So the yogi refuses. Quietly. No speech, no triumph. Notice who's at the door. Not enemies. Gods, and good things: long life, beauty, ease. A generous invitation can be harder to turn down than a hostile one. And on an ordinary Tuesday? The invitation is rarely a flying chariot. It's the comfortable stopping place, just short of what you set out to do.
screen: `SARVA-JNATRITVA: KNOWING EVERYTHING.` · `DISPASSION, EVEN TOWARD THAT.` · `NO ATTACHMENT. NO PRIDE.` · `THE LAMP AND THE WIND.` · then, large: `REFUSE THE INVITATION.`

segments.voice: Today's practice notices the comfortable stopping places. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. After a while, something pleasant will invite you away: a daydream, a plan for later, a drowsy warmth. Notice it like a kind visitor at the door. You don't have to be rude to it. Just thank it, silently, and stay with the breath. If a little pride follows at having stayed, greet it the same way, and let it pass. The bell holds the time.
Omniscience. Knowing everything, which comes from full discernment, and which Patanjali says to let go of too.
Your line: refuse the invitation. Today, when a comfortable reason to stop short shows up, decline it kindly once, without feeling proud that you did. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often tell the Bhashya's scene of the gods' invitation to warn students against both attachment and pride in their progress, and Hindu stories praise renunciants who turn down heavenly rewards for the sake of liberation.

fork.setup: the gods invite you to stay in their world, with an elixir against age and death. what does sutra 3.51 say?
options: decline, and be proud the gods came for you.
decline, without attachment and without pride.
fork.reveal: 3.51: no attachment and no pride, since unwanted things could return. the commentary's yogi won't let sweet things be the wind that blows out the lamp of yoga.

original.note: Sanskrit sarva-jñātṛtva: being the knower (jñātṛ) of all (sarva), omniscience, 3.49.

trapdoor: what you thought: the goal of yoga is to know everything.
what it means: even omniscience is set down; then the gods' invitation is refused, without clinging and without pride.
what a scholar hears: tad-vairagyad api (3.50); sthany-upanimantrane sanga-smaya-akaranam (3.51); the Bhashya's four kinds of yogi, with the invitation coming at the second stage.

notes: The gods' speech and the yogi's reflection (roasted on the coals of samsara; the lamp of yoga and the wind of sense objects) are paraphrased from memory of the Bhashya on 3.51; confirm.
'Discernment, which we met three weeks ago' refers to day 456 (2.26).

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed 'you've earned it' from the gods' speech (not in the Bhashya's list) and the screen; cut two superlatives ('the most flattering invitation anyone has ever received', 'the boldest line'); fixed 'two weeks ago' to three (day 456); varied the practice so it no longer repeats day 473's 'something you did well' thought.
The Bhashya's four classes of yogi (the invitation comes to the madhu-bhumika stage) is mentioned only in the trapdoor.
